title: Move your body
hook: regular movement has solid evidence for lifting mild low mood

segments.voice: Yesterday: sleep first. Did you keep your bedtime last night, or did the one-more-episode voice win? Either way, tonight is another try. Day three hundred twenty-one.

A gray afternoon. Nothing is exactly wrong, but everything feels heavy. The couch is right there. Your phone is right there. The idea of putting on shoes and going outside feels about as possible as climbing a mountain. And yet, most of us have had this experience: you drag yourself out anyway, you walk around the block, and you come back just a little lighter. Not fixed. Lighter. For a long time that was just something people said. Now there's a large pile of careful studies behind it. Today: move your body.
screen: `A GRAY, HEAVY AFTERNOON.` → `AROUND THE BLOCK ANYWAY.` → `JUST A LITTLE LIGHTER.`

segments.voice: First, the evidence. Researchers have run many trials where people with low mood are assigned to exercise, often walking, jogging, strength training or yoga, and compared with people who aren't. Pulled together, these trials find that regular movement reliably lifts mild to moderate low mood, with effects that in some reviews look comparable to other common treatments. The quality of the studies varies, and many are small, so reviewers stay careful. But among the practices we've looked at this year, this is one of the best supported. Second, how much. The trials don't require marathons. Brisk walking a few times a week has shown benefits. More vigorous movement seems to help somewhat more, but the best amount is the one you'll actually do. Remember easy beats heroic. Third, a caution that matters. If low mood is heavy, lasts for weeks, or comes with thoughts of harming yourself, movement isn't a replacement for real help. Talk to a doctor or someone you trust. Fourth, the old movers. Aristotle's students were called the Peripatetics, from the Greek for a covered walkway at their school, and the story grew that he taught while walking. Rumi's followers, the Mevlevi, turn in their famous whirling prayer. Buddhist monks practice walking meditation. Pilgrims in many traditions walk for weeks. The Danish philosopher Kierkegaard wrote to a relative that he had walked himself into his best thoughts, and knew of no burden so heavy that one couldn't walk away from it. Your body isn't the vehicle that carries the real you to the practice. Sometimes it is the practice.
screen: `MOVEMENT LIFTS MILD LOW MOOD.` · `THE BEST AMOUNT IS THE ONE YOU DO.` · `HEAVY OR LASTING? GET REAL HELP.` · `THE PERIPATETICS, THE TURNERS.` · then, large: `MOVE.`

segments.voice: Stand up, if you can. Roll your shoulders back, slowly, three times. Lift your arms overhead and stretch, then let them fall. Now walk, around the room, or in place, at an easy pace. Feel each foot land. If standing isn't possible, move what you can: hands, shoulders, the breath. Then decide on twenty minutes of moving later today. The bell holds the time.
Move your body. Regular movement, even brisk walking, has some of the strongest evidence of any practice for lifting mild low mood. Today's word.
Your line: move. Twenty minutes today, any kind: a brisk walk, dancing in the kitchen, the stairs instead of the elevator. After your cue, if you like. Day three hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Many people use a daily walk, run, swim or class to steady their mood; many traditions include moving practices, from walking meditation and pilgrimage to yoga and the Mevlevi turning.

fork.reveal: small, regular movement helps, and the best amount is the one you actually do. you don't need to feel like it first.

notes: Exercise and depression: Cochrane 2013 found moderate effects vs control, comparable to psychological or drug treatment in the few trials that compared them, with lower-quality evidence; Noetel et al. 2024 found walking/jogging, yoga and strength training effective, more so at higher intensity. Confirm the script's summary, including 'comparable to other common treatments' hedged as 'in some reviews'.
Kierkegaard letter (1847, to his sister-in-law Henriette Lund): paraphrased; confirm recipient and wording.
Peripatetic: from peripatos, the covered walk at the Lyceum; the 'taught while walking' story is traditional and disputed. Script says 'the story grew'.
Mevlevi sema described as 'whirling prayer'; a Sufi reviewer may prefer 'the sema, a turning ceremony of remembrance'.
